intro: Four contrasting sections move from march to quick dance, slow declamation and an octave-driven finale. Listen for the changes of pace as well as the changes of register.
question: How does repeated octave writing turn a tune into momentum?

sections.label: Octave variations
sections.mNote: dance tune doubled in octaves with denser repeated attacks

relations.label: The quick dance repeats
relations.basis: The Presto dance is a repeated unit between the opening march and the Andante. Both excerpts fall within the 85–126 s Presto region rather than in the later octave variations. CENS diagonal mean 0.989, sustained 18.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 18.5 s (cache/form/liszt-hungarian-rhapsody-6.txt, candidate 1; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Four sections, one pianist
cues.text: The opening has the measured tread of a march. Liszt sets it beside a quick dance, a slower song and an extended fast finale; the contrasts of pace are part of the design, not interruptions of it.
cues.evidence: The score gives the contrasting tempo headings. Leslie Howard’s Hyperion notes describe the work’s four-section design.

cues.title: Published in a larger group
cues.text: The sixth rhapsody appeared in 1853, alongside Nos. 3–15. Liszt reused and reshaped material from his earlier Hungarian pieces rather than composing the whole collection from newly invented melodies.
cues.evidence: Leslie Howard’s Hyperion notes document the publication group and its earlier sources: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9

cues.title: Between march and dance
cues.text: Around the transition out of the opening section, listen for the contrast between measured phrases and freer, more rapid passagework. The changing pace helps separate the rhapsody’s sections.
cues.evidence: The report shows a withdrawal around 1:05–1:10, quicker attacks around 1:15 and a renewed phrase around 1:25. The score places a quick section after the opening march.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Sources beyond one tradition
cues.text: The rhapsodies draw on songs, published dances and the improvisatory playing of Romani musicians. Their material is not a single body of anonymous rural folk song: composed melodies and performing traditions both contributed.
cues.evidence: Howard distinguishes folk material, published compositions and Romani improvisation in his Hyperion account: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9

cues.title: The slower song
cues.text: The Andante gives the melody more room for pauses and ornament after the quick section. Listen for a longer line spanning those pauses rather than a succession of unrelated flourishes.
cues.evidence: The score places the slow section third. A measured change around 2:06 and fewer attacks through 2:15 suggest its start, without locating each phrase.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: A song before Liszt
cues.text: The slow section’s melody is by Ádám Pálóczi Horváth and was published in 1813. Liszt had already used it in his earlier “Rumanian Rhapsody”. Its apparently improvisatory setting therefore contains a tune with a documented printed history.
cues.evidence: Howard identifies the composer, publication date and earlier Liszt use in the notes on Rhapsody VI: https://www.hyperion-records.co.uk/dc.asp?dc=D_CDA67418%2F9

cues.title: Activity and a quiet gap
cues.text: Near the end of the slow span, freer passagework separates the song from the fast finale. Listen through the quicker activity to the quieter space before the next sustained dance rhythm.
cues.evidence: The report shows rapid activity around 3:50, followed by very low level around 4:00–4:05. This is compatible with the score’s transition, not a precise cadenza boundary.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The fast final dance
cues.text: The final dance establishes a repeated rhythmic support in B♭ major. Listen for that foundation while the melodic writing becomes increasingly elaborate.
cues.evidence: The score’s fast final section follows the Andante. Increasing attacks and B♭-centred pitch estimates around 4:10–4:25 suggest a start around 4:08.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The octave writing
cues.text: In the finale’s repeated-octave passages, the same pitch is doubled at the octave while the hand repeats and moves as a unit. Try to follow the tune through the repeated attacks rather than treating the technique as the whole musical point.
cues.evidence: Repeated octaves are written in the finale. The report shows a sustained increase in attacks around 4:50–5:15, compatible with this placement but not a note-by-note alignment.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: More than fast notes
cues.text: Through the fuller final stretch, follow the longer phrase beneath the repeated attacks. A change in register or emphasis can shape the melody even while the small notes keep moving.
cues.evidence: This is a listening suggestion for the score’s octave-driven finale. The report shows a sustained high relative level around 5:20–5:45; it does not measure the pianist’s phrasing.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: A different home key
cues.text: The rhapsody finishes in B♭ major rather than the D♭ major of the opening. Compare the final dance’s tonal destination with the march that began the piece.
cues.evidence: The opening and final keys come from the score. B♭, D and F dominate the closing recorded span around 5:55–6:10, before the level drops around 6:15.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The flourish releases a lighter dance
transitions.how: The march’s firm chordal tread loosens into a keyboard flourish before the Presto begins with lighter, more regular movement. D♭ major is respelt C♯ major: the notation changes, but the tonic pitch does not. Liszt therefore makes speed, articulation and texture announce the new section rather than a distant modulation. The broad bass-and-chord support gives way to the quick dance’s compact accompaniment, leaving more space around the upper line.
transitions.evidence: The Presto marker is 1:25. Analysis shows withdrawal at 1:05–1:10, faster attacks at 1:15 and a quieter reset at 1:25; the provisional relation matches the following dance twice. The score supplies the flourish, Presto heading and enharmonic D♭/C♯ notation. The key spelling is not inferred from the analyser’s C♯ label.

transitions.title: The dance cadence gives way to speech
transitions.how: The quick dance completes its repeated paragraph, then the Andante turns to B♭ minor, the relative minor of the opening D♭ major. Liszt removes the Presto’s continuous motion and lets a slower melody speak across spaces in the accompaniment. Ornament and pauses stretch the phrase while the piano’s lower notes supply intermittent harmonic support. The common notes D♭ and F link the tonal worlds, but the new pace and declamatory delivery make the seam unmistakable.
transitions.evidence: The Andante boundary is 2:06, a measured change; level and attack density fall around 2:05–2:15. The repeated Presto relation ends near 2:05.5. The score supplies the B♭-minor slow section and its ornamented, interrupted phrase structure; shared chord notes are described without asserting a particular pivot chord.

transitions.title: F prepares a new major-key dance
transitions.how: The slow song ends in freer passagework that gathers around F, the dominant of B♭. After the flourish and withdrawal, the Allegro establishes B♭ major: D♮ replaces the slow section’s D♭. A regular bass-and-chord pattern now fixes the dance pulse beneath the tune. The new major third and the measured accompaniment turn the same tonic into a different kind of music, preparing the repeated-octave variations rather than beginning with their full weight.
transitions.evidence: The Allegro boundary is 4:08, also a measured change. Rapid activity near 3:50 gives way to very low level at 4:00–4:05, followed by B♭-centred sound and renewed attacks. The written cadenza, F-dominant preparation and B♭-major friss supply the harmonic explanation; neither the last flourish note nor the first dance attack is aligned.

transitions.title: The tune becomes repeated octaves
transitions.how: The dance does not need another key to intensify. In the B♭-major finale, Liszt doubles the melodic line in octaves and increases its repeated attacks while the left hand preserves the bass-and-chord rhythm. The tune still moves in phrases larger than the individual repetitions. Wider spacing and denser articulation change the piano’s weight, so the listener can hear a variation beginning even though the underlying dance and tonal destination remain recognisable.
transitions.evidence: The octave-variation marker is 4:48, a measured boundary. Detected attacks increase to roughly seven per second at 4:50–5:00, alongside a rise in relative level. Repeated melodic octaves over rhythmic bass support are written features of the finale; the relation file correctly treats this as variation rather than a verified literal repeat.

transitions.title: Contrary motion closes the keyboard’s span
transitions.how: The final drive compresses the dance into closing display. Octave writing spreads across the keyboard, and chromatic scales in contrary motion pull the hands apart before the concluding B♭-major chords. The bass no longer merely marks steps beneath a tune: both registers participate in the rush towards the cadence. Liszt closes in the friss’s B♭ major, not the march’s D♭, making the last dance’s destination govern the whole ending.
transitions.evidence: The final-drive marker is 5:55, near the measured change at 5:52. B♭-centred windows continue through 6:10, followed by the terminal decay. The score supplies the contrary-motion chromatic octave scales and B♭-major closing chords; their individual attacks are not aligned to this marker.

facts: Piano with Carl Czerny and composition with Antonio Salieri in Vienna; later composition with Anton Reicha in Paris
Weimar masterclasses; first president of the Hungarian Royal Academy of Music, founded in 1875
Piano music and transcriptions; thirteen symphonic poems; two programme symphonies; concertos, songs and sacred music
composer.background:
Liszt was born in Doborján, a German-speaking village in the Hungarian kingdom, where his father Adam worked on an Esterházy estate. Hungary remained his declared homeland, although German and French were his principal languages. Adam taught him piano before taking him to Vienna in 1822 for lessons with Carl Czerny, who had studied with Beethoven, and Antonio Salieri. The family moved to Paris the following year. The Conservatoire refused him admission as a foreigner; private teaching and public concerts supplied his education instead. His early career therefore joined two institutions that would remain distinct in his adult life: the disciplined lesson and the commercial concert platform.

Adam died in 1827, leaving the sixteen-year-old Liszt to support himself and his mother by teaching. Paris offered an education beyond the keyboard: Victor Hugo, the religious social thinker Félicité de Lamennais, Chopin and Berlioz belonged to his intellectual or musical circle. Hearing Paganini in 1832 suggested that a pianist might make technical difficulty carry the same theatrical force as the violinist’s leaps and harmonics. Liszt responded with prolonged practice and transcription: his piano version of Berlioz’s Symphonie fantastique, published in 1834, aimed to preserve orchestral detail.
composer.born: 22 October 1811, Doborján, Kingdom of Hungary (now Raiding, Austria)
composer.epithet: The touring pianist who made a single theme change character, and eventually stripped virtuosity down to a few unresolved notes.
